learningObjectives.title: Solids, liquids and gases: particle arrangement and properties
Changes of state and the kinetic particle model
Effects of temperature and pressure on gases

questions.q: Which state of matter has both a fixed shape and a fixed volume?
questions.explain: In a solid the particles are held in fixed positions by strong forces, giving a fixed shape and fixed volume.

questions.q: In which state are the particles far apart and moving randomly at high speed?
questions.explain: Gas particles have widely spaced, negligible forces between them and move quickly in random directions.

questions.q: Why can a liquid flow and take the shape of its container?
options: Its particles can move and slide past one another
Its particles are held in fixed positions
Its particles are very far apart
Its particles have no forces between them
questions.explain: Liquid particles are still close together but are free to move past each other, allowing the liquid to flow.

questions.q: How are the particles arranged in a solid?
options: Closely packed in a regular pattern, vibrating about fixed positions
Closely packed but arranged randomly and able to move
Widely spaced and moving randomly at speed
In a regular pattern but far apart
questions.explain: Solid particles are held in a fixed, ordered arrangement and can only vibrate in place.

questions.q: Why can gases be compressed much more easily than solids or liquids?
options: There are large spaces between the gas particles
The gas particles are held in a regular pattern
The gas particles have strong forces between them
questions.explain: Because gas particles are far apart, they can be pushed closer together, so gases are easily compressed.

questions.q: What is the name of the change of state from a liquid to a gas that occurs throughout the liquid at a fixed temperature?
questions.explain: Boiling is the change from liquid to gas that takes place throughout the liquid at its boiling point.

questions.q: What is the name of the change when a solid turns directly into a gas without becoming a liquid?
questions.explain: Sublimation is the direct change of a solid into a gas without passing through the liquid state.

questions.q: The change of state from a gas to a liquid is called:
questions.explain: Condensation is the change from gas to liquid, occurring when a gas is cooled.

questions.q: What happens to the particles when a solid is heated and melts?
options: They gain energy, vibrate more and overcome the forces holding them in place
They lose energy and move closer together
They gain energy but stay in fixed positions
questions.explain: Heating gives the particles enough energy to break out of their fixed positions, so the solid melts into a liquid.

questions.q: During freezing, what happens to the energy of the particles?
options: Energy is released as the particles slow down and settle into fixed positions
Energy is absorbed as the particles speed up
Energy is released as the particles move further apart
questions.explain: As a liquid freezes, particles lose kinetic energy, slow down and become fixed in the solid arrangement.

questions.q: A substance melts at -7 degrees C and boils at 58 degrees C. What is its state at 25 degrees C?
questions.explain: At 25 degrees C the temperature is above the melting point but below the boiling point, so the substance is a liquid.

questions.q: A sealed, rigid metal cylinder of gas is heated. What happens to the gas pressure inside it?
questions.explain: Heating makes the particles move faster and hit the walls more often and harder, so at fixed volume the pressure rises.

questions.q: Why does the pressure of a gas increase when its volume is reduced at constant temperature?
options: The particles hit the container walls more frequently
questions.explain: In a smaller volume the particles collide with the walls more often, increasing the pressure.

questions.q: What effect does increasing the temperature have on the motion of gas particles?
options: They gain kinetic energy and move faster
They lose energy and move slower
They move at the same speed but get bigger
questions.explain: Raising the temperature increases the average kinetic energy of the particles, so they move faster.

questions.q: Which statement best describes diffusion?
options: The net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration
The movement of particles from low to high concentration
The change of a liquid into a gas
The packing of particles into a regular pattern
questions.explain: Diffusion is the spreading of particles due to their random motion, from where they are more concentrated to where they are less concentrated.

questions.q: Why does diffusion occur faster in gases than in liquids?
options: Gas particles move faster and are further apart
Gas particles are held in fixed positions
Gas particles have stronger forces between them
questions.explain: Faster-moving, widely spaced gas particles can spread out more quickly than the closer, slower liquid particles.

questions.q: For gases at the same temperature, which particles diffuse fastest?
options: Those with the lower relative molecular mass
Those with the higher relative molecular mass
All gases diffuse at exactly the same rate
questions.explain: Lighter particles (lower relative molecular mass) travel faster and so diffuse more quickly at the same temperature.

questions.q: Cotton wool soaked in ammonia solution (giving NH3, Mr 17) and in hydrochloric acid (giving HCl, Mr 36.5) are placed at opposite ends of a glass tube. Where does the white ring of ammonium chloride form?
questions.explain: NH3 has the lower Mr so it diffuses faster and travels further, meeting the slower HCl nearer the acid end.

questions.q: What happens to the rate of diffusion if the temperature is increased?
questions.explain: At a higher temperature particles have more kinetic energy and move faster, so they diffuse more quickly.

questions.q: Hydrogen (Mr 2) and oxygen (Mr 32) are released at the same point. Which gas diffuses faster?
options: They diffuse at the same rate
questions.explain: Hydrogen has the much lower relative molecular mass, so its particles move faster and it diffuses more quickly.
